module_title: Selecting Fodder Crops for African Conditions

lessons.title: Best Grasses for Hay: Rhodes, Napier, and Guinea Grass
lessons.body:
Rhodes grass (Chloris gayana) is a drought-tolerant perennial that grows well in dry areas with 400â800 mm annual rainfall. It establishes quickly from seed, and you can cut it 3â4 times per year. For hay, cut at early flowering when protein is around 8â10%. Yields range from 8â15 tonnes dry matter per hectare per year. It needs good drainage; waterlogging kills it. Common varieties: Katambora, Samford, and Nemkat. Fertilize with 50 kg/ha nitrogen after each cut if you want high yields.

Napier grass (Pennisetum purpureum), also called elephant grass, is a tall, high-yielding perennial. It can produce 20â40 tonnes dry matter per hectare per year under good management. Plant using stem cuttings (3-node pieces) spaced 50 cm x 100 cm. It needs 800â1500 mm rainfall or irrigation. Cut every 6â8 weeks for hay or silage. For hay, cut at 1â1.5 m height; for silage, 1.5â2 m. It is not drought-tolerant but responds well to manure and nitrogen. Watch for Napier stunt disease; use resistant varieties like South African or French Cameroon.

Guinea grass (Panicum maximum) is a tufted perennial that grows in humid and sub-humid areas (700â1200 mm rainfall). It yields 10â20 tonnes dry matter per hectare per year. It is shade-tolerant and can be intercropped with trees. Cut for hay at 60â90 cm height before seed heads form. It recovers quickly after cutting. Varieties: Mombasa, Tanzania, and Gatton. It needs moderate fertility; apply 40 kg/ha nitrogen after each cut. Guinea grass is less tolerant of waterlogging than Napier.

For all three grasses, make hay when 3â5 days of dry, sunny weather are forecast. Cut in the morning after dew has dried. Spread in a thin layer and turn daily. Bale when moisture is 15â18%. Store in a dry, raised shed. In Africa, Rhodes is best for dry areas, Napier for high-rainfall or irrigated areas, and Guinea for humid zones. Always test your soil first; add lime if pH is below 5.5.

lessons.title: Legumes for Hay: Lucerne, Desmodium, and Lablab
lessons.body:
Lucerne (alfalfa, Medicago sativa) is the top legume for hay in Africa, especially in cooler, high-altitude areas (above 1000 m) with irrigation. It yields 10â15 tonnes dry matter per hectare per year. It needs well-drained soil with pH 6.5â7.5. Inoculate seed with Rhizobium meliloti before planting. Sow 20â25 kg/ha in rows 30 cm apart. Cut at 10% flowering for hay; protein is 16â20%. Let it flower once a year to maintain stand. It is deep-rooted and drought-tolerant but not for waterlogged or acidic soils. Common varieties: Hunter River, CUF 101, and local selections.

Desmodium (Desmodium intortum and D. uncinatum) is a trailing legume that grows in humid and sub-humid areas (800â1500 mm rainfall). It yields 5â10 tonnes dry matter per hectare per year. It is shade-tolerant and works well in mixed pastures with grasses like Napier or Guinea. For hay, cut at early flowering when protein is 14â18%. It is difficult to dry because stems are thick; condition with a roller-crimper or dry in small racks. Desmodium fixes nitrogen and improves soil. It can be aggressive and climb over crops. Plant using seed at 2â4 kg/ha or cuttings.

Lablab (Lablab purpureus) is an annual legume that grows in a wide range of climates, including semi-arid areas with 600â1200 mm rainfall. It yields 4â8 tonnes dry matter per hectare per year. It is often intercropped with maize or sorghum for silage. For hay, cut at pod formation when protein is 15â18%. It is drought-tolerant and fixes nitrogen. Sow 20â30 kg/ha in rows 50â75 cm apart. It can be grazed or cut. Varieties: Rongai, Highworth, and local types. Lablab hay is palatable and good for dairy cows.

For all legumes, dry hay quickly to avoid leaf loss. Leaves are the most nutritious part. Use a mower-conditioner or turn frequently. Bale at 15â18% moisture. Store in a dry place. In Africa, lucerne is best for highlands with irrigation, desmodium for humid zones, and lablab for dry areas and intercropping. Always mix legumes with grasses for balanced hay.

lessons.title: High-Yield Crops for Silage: Maize, Sorghum, and Millet
lessons.body:
Maize (Zea mays) is the best crop for silage in Africa because of its high energy and yields. A good hybrid can produce 40â60 tonnes fresh weight per hectare, or 15â20 tonnes dry matter. Plant at 75 cm between rows and 25 cm within rows (about 53,000 plants/ha). Use high-yielding hybrids like DK, SC, or local improved varieties. Apply 100â150 kg/ha nitrogen in split doses: half at planting, half at knee height. For silage, harvest when kernels are at dough stage (30â35% dry matter). Chop to 1â2 cm lengths. Maize silage has 30â35% starch and 8â10% protein. It ferments well. In dry areas, use drought-tolerant varieties like Katumani or local composites.

Sorghum (Sorghum bicolor) is more drought-tolerant than maize and yields 20â40 tonnes fresh weight per hectare. It is ideal for semi-arid areas (400â800 mm rainfall). Plant at 60 cm x 20 cm. Use sweet sorghum or forage sorghum varieties like Sugardrip, Jowar, or local. Apply 60â80 kg/ha nitrogen. Harvest at soft dough stage (30â35% dry matter). Chop finely. Sorghum silage has 10â12% protein and good energy. Some varieties have prussic acid (HCN) when stressed; wilt for 24 hours before ensiling to reduce risk. Sorghum can also be mixed with lablab or cowpea for higher protein.

Millet (pearl millet, Pennisetum glaucum) is the most drought-tolerant of the three. It yields 15â25 tonnes fresh weight per hectare in areas with 300â600 mm rainfall. Plant at 75 cm x 20 cm. Use varieties like ICMV, Okashana, or local. Apply 40â60 kg/ha nitrogen. Harvest at dough stage. Chop to 1â2 cm. Millet silage has 8â10% protein and good energy. It is often mixed with legumes like groundnut haulms or lablab to improve protein. Millet stover is also used for hay or bedding.

For all three, wilt to 30â35% dry matter before chopping. Add molasses at 2â5% if sugar is low. Pack tightly in a silo pit or bunker, cover with plastic, and seal. Use within 6 months. In Africa, maize is best for high-rainfall or irrigated areas, sorghum for medium rainfall, and millet for dry areas.

lessons.title: Using Crop Residues: Maize Stover, Rice Straw, and Groundnut Haulms
lessons.body:
Maize stover is the stalks, leaves, and cobs left after harvesting grain. It is the most common crop residue in Africa. Yields are 2â4 tonnes dry matter per hectare. It has low protein (3â5%) and high fibre, so it is best for maintenance, not weight gain. To make hay, cut stover while still green (after cob harvest but before leaves dry). Dry to 15â18% moisture and bale. For silage, chop and ensile with molasses (5%) or mix with legumes like lablab. Stover can be treated with urea (4 kg urea in 100 L water per 100 kg stover) to raise protein to 8â10% and improve digestibility. Store under cover.

Rice straw is the stems and leaves left after rice harvest. It yields 2â5 tonnes dry matter per hectare. It is very low in protein (3â4%) and high in silica, making it less digestible than maize stover. It is best used as bedding or mixed with other feeds. For hay, dry and bale. For silage, chop and mix with high-protein crops like lucerne or desmodium. Treat with urea (same rate as maize stover) to improve quality. Rice straw is often burned in fields; instead, collect and store it. It can be fed to cattle, but supplement with protein and energy.

Groundnut haulms are the vines and leaves left after harvesting groundnuts. They are high in protein (10â15%) and highly digestible. They are excellent for hay and silage. Yields are 1â3 tonnes dry matter per hectare. For hay, dry quickly in the sun and bale. For silage, mix with maize or sorghum at 20â30% to boost protein. Groundnut haulms are best fed to dairy cows, goats, and sheep. They are also a good source of calcium. Store in a dry place; they are prone to mould. Do not feed mouldy haulms; they can cause aflatoxin poisoning.

In Africa, crop residues are often wasted or burned. Instead, collect, dry, and store them. Use a shed or cover with tarpaulin. For silage, chop to 2â3 cm and pack tightly. Mix residues with legumes or treat with urea to improve nutrition. Always test for mould before feeding.

lessons.title: Drought-Tolerant Fodder Crops for Arid Regions
lessons.body:
In arid and semi-arid regions of Africa (less than 500 mm rainfall), you need fodder crops that survive long dry spells. The best options are pearl millet, sorghum, Rhodes grass, and drought-tolerant legumes like lablab and cowpea. Pearl millet is the most drought-tolerant cereal; it yields 15â25 tonnes fresh weight per hectare with 300â500 mm rainfall. Plant at 75 cm x 20 cm after the first rains. Use early-maturing varieties like Okashana 1 or ICMV 221. Harvest at dough stage for silage. It can also be cut for hay.

Sorghum is another good choice. Use drought-tolerant varieties like Gadam, Serena, or local. It yields 20â30 tonnes fresh weight per hectare. Plant at 60 cm x 20 cm. It can stay green in dry spells. Harvest at soft dough. For hay, cut at boot stage. Sorghum can accumulate prussic acid in drought; wilt before feeding. Rhodes grass is a perennial that survives dry seasons. It yields 8â12 tonnes dry matter per hectare. Plant seed at 5â10 kg/ha. It needs good drainage. Cut for hay at early flowering.

Legumes for arid areas: Lablab (Lablab purpureus) is drought-tolerant and yields 4â8 tonnes dry matter per hectare. It can be intercropped with millet or sorghum. Cowpea (Vigna unguiculata) is another drought-tolerant legume. It yields 2â5 tonnes dry matter per hectare. For hay, cut at pod formation. Both fix nitrogen and improve soil. Other options: pigeon pea (Cajanus cajan) and Dolichos lablab. These can be cut for hay or silage.

Water conservation is key. Use zai pits, half-moons, or contour ridges to capture rainwater. Mulch to reduce evaporation. Plant drought-tolerant crops in basins. Harvest and store fodder when green. In very dry areas, consider cactus (Opuntia) as a fodder source; it is 90% water and survives with 200 mm rainfall. Spineless cactus varieties are best. Chop and mix with dry roughage. Always provide water and shade for animals. In arid regions, fodder banks of these crops can save livestock during droughts.

lessons.title: Mixing Crops for Balanced Nutrition in Silage
lessons.body:
Silage made from a single crop often lacks balanced nutrition. For example, maize silage is high in energy but low in protein (8â10%). Legume silage is high in protein but low in energy. Mixing crops at ensiling gives a balanced feed. The goal is 14â16% protein and 30â35% dry matter. A common mix in Africa is 70% maize or sorghum and 30% lablab or cowpea. This raises protein to 12â14%. Another mix: 60% Napier grass, 20% desmodium, and 20% maize. This gives good energy and protein.

When mixing, chop all crops to 1â2 cm. Mix thoroughly. Aim for 30â35% dry matter. If too wet, wilt; if too dry, add water or fresh material. Add molasses at 2â5% if sugar is low. For high-protein mixes, add 3â5% salt to improve palatability. Pack tightly in a silo pit or bunker. Cover with plastic and seal. Fermentation takes 3â6 weeks. Good silage smells sweet and acidic, not rancid.

Example recipe for 1 tonne of mixed silage: 700 kg chopped maize (dough stage), 250 kg chopped lablab (pod stage), 50 kg molasses, and 5 kg salt. Mix well. This gives about 13% protein and 65% TDN. Another recipe: 500 kg Napier grass, 300 kg desmodium, 200 kg maize stover, 50 kg molasses. This is good for dairy cows. For dry season feeding, mix 50% sorghum silage with 50% groundnut haulms silage.

Always test your silage before feeding. Use a pH meter or litmus paper; good silage has pH 3.8â4.5. If pH is above 5, it may spoil. Feed 15â20 kg per dairy cow per day, plus dry hay. For goats and sheep, feed 2â3 kg per day. Mixing crops also spreads risk: if one crop fails, others may survive. In Africa, intercropping maize with lablab or cowpea in the field and then ensiling together is a practical way to get balanced silage. Plant maize at 75 cm rows and lablab between rows. Harvest together at dough stage. This saves labour and improves feed quality.

lessons.title: Practical Reference
lessons.body:
Practical Reference: Selecting Fodder Crops for African Conditions

Fodder crop selection is one of the highest-leverage decisions an African livestock or dairy enterprise makes. The right crop can cut purchased feed costs by 40â60%, extend the grazing season through the dry months, and turn a smallholder operation into a commercially viable business. The wrong crop wastes land, labour, and capital for an entire season. This reference lesson gives you the decision tools, yield benchmarks, and safety rules you need to select fodder crops matched to your agro-ecological zone, your animals, and your market.

Across sub-Saharan Africa, the dominant constraint is not land â it is the dry season. Most smallholder herds lose 15â25% of body weight between November and March, and milk yields can fall by half. Well-made hay and silage bridge that gap. But the crop you choose to conserve determines whether you bridge it profitably or expensively. Use the tables and checklist below as your field decision aid.

Yield and Suitability Benchmarks

The table below summarises expected dry matter (DM) yields under rain-fed smallholder and semi-commercial conditions in East and Southern Africa. Use it to compare expected output against your land, rainfall, and labour. Yields vary with soil fertility, variety, and management â treat these as planning benchmarks, not guarantees.

Table 1: Fodder crop yield & suitability benchmarks â African conditions
Crop Type Rainfall need (mm) DM yield (t/ha/yr) Best use Key limitation
Rhodes grassGrass400â8008â15HayNeeds fertile soil, slow establishment
Napier grassGrass700â150015â40Silage / fresh chopHigh water & nutrient demand
Guinea grassGrass600â120010â25Hay / grazingBecomes stemmy if cut late
Lucerne (alfalfa)Legume500â900 (irrig.)8â18Hay, proteinNeeds deep, drained, limed soil
DesmodiumLegume700â15004â10Hay, mixed silageSlow to dry, mould risk
LablabLegume500â9005â12Hay, silage mixShort-season, needs support
Maize (forage)Cereal600â120015â30SilageSingle cut, high input cost
Sorghum (forage)Cereal400â90012â25SilagePrussic acid risk in young regrowth
Pearl milletCereal300â7008â18Silage, hayLower energy than maize

Sources: FAO Grassland Index species datasheets (FAO, 2023); ILRI/CIAT tropical forage database (2019); AIC (Kenya) fodder agronomy notes (2021).

Nutritional Quality and Conservation Fit

Yield alone does not determine profitability. Crude protein (CP), digestibility, and how well a crop conserves determine actual feed value. Legumes raise protein; grasses give bulk energy. For silage, you need adequate water-soluble carbohydrates (WSC) for fermentation â cereals have this, pure legumes usually do not and must be mixed.

Table 2: Feed quality and conservation characteristics
Crop Crude protein (% DM) Digestibility Hay suitability Silage suitability Notes for African farms
Rhodes grass7â11MediumExcellentPoor aloneDries fast; mix with legume for protein
Napier grass8â14MediumâhighFairGood (chopped)Cut at 1â1.2 m for quality
Guinea grass7â12MediumGoodFairWidely adapted, good for cut-and-carry
Lucerne16â22HighExcellentPoor aloneBest protein hay; needs lime & drainage
Desmodium14â20HighFairGood in mixExcellent with Napier or maize
Lablab14â20HighGoodGood in mixDrought escape; fixes nitrogen
Maize silage7â9High (grain)PoorExcellentHigh energy; add legume for protein
Sorghum silage8â11MediumâhighPoorExcellentDrought-hardy; watch prussic acid
Maize stover3â5LowPoorFair (treated)Ammonia/urea treatment raises value
Rice straw3â5LowPoorFair (treated)Abundant in rice zones; treat before use
Groundnut haulms10â14MediumGoodFairHigh-value residue; store dry, off ground

Sources: Feedipedia animal feed composition tables (INRAE/CIRAD/AFZ, 2022); FAO Tropical Feeds (2020); ILRI FEAST feed quality data (2019).

Mixing for Balanced Silage

A profitable silage pit is rarely a single crop. The standard African commercial mix is 70â80% cereal (maize or sorghum) for energy and fermentable sugar, plus 20â30% legume (lablab, desmodium, or lucerne) for protein. Target 30â35% dry matter at ensiling, chop to 1â2 cm, and compact in thin layers. This produces silage with 12â16% CP â enough to support milk yields of 15â20 litres/day without expensive concentrate. For arid regions, sorghum-millet mixes with lablab give reliable tonnage where maize fails.

â ï¸ SAFETY WARNING â Prussic Acid (HCN) in Sorghum & Sudangrass

Young, drought-stressed, or frost-damaged sorghum, sudangrass, and sorghum-sudan hybrids can accumulate toxic levels of hydrocyanic acid (prussic acid) that kill cattle within hours. Never graze or feed fresh regrowth under 45 cm tall, or within 2 weeks after drought stress or frost. Always wilt chopped material for 24â48 hours before ensiling â ensiling reduces HCN but does not eliminate it. Test suspect forage before feeding. Symptoms include rapid breathing, staggering, muscle tremors, and sudden death. Call a vet immediately if observed. Groundnut haulms must also be checked for aflatoxin mould before feeding.

Business Considerations for African Producers

Treat fodder as a business line, not a by-product. Key commercial levers:

  • Cost per kg DM: Rhodes grass hay typically costs US$0.08â0.15/kg DM to produce vs US$0.25â0.40/kg for purchased dairy meal. The margin is your profit.
  • Land efficiency: Napier under irrigation can out-yield open grazing 5â10Ã. On 1 hectare you can support 2â3 dairy cows year-round.
  • Market demand: Urban dairy belts (Nairobi, Addis Ababa, Kampala, Dar es Salaam, Lagos) pay premium prices for consistent, well-baled hay and sealed silage.
  • Seed and input access: Source certified seed from national research bodies (KALRO, EIAR, NARO, IITA) to avoid counterfeit varieties and poor germination.
  • Value addition: Chopping, baling, and urea treatment of residues can raise sale price 30â60%.

Quick Reference Checklist

  1. Match crop to rainfall zone â do not plant Napier or lucerne in <600 mm areas without irrigation.
  2. Test soil pH and fertility first â most fodder grasses and legumes need pH 5.8â7.0 and adequate phosphorus.
  3. Plan for the dry season â target at least 3 months of conserved feed per animal before the rains end.
  4. Always mix cereal + legume for silage â 70â80% cereal, 20â30% legume for balanced energy and protein.
  5. Harvest at the right stage â grasses at pre-flowering, cereals at dough stage, legumes at early pod for best quality.
  6. Wilt before ensiling â target 30â35% DM to prevent poor fermentation and effluent loss.
  7. Store residues off the ground â protect stover, straw, and haulms from rain, termites, and mould.
  8. Never feed stressed sorghum regrowth â observe the 45 cm and 2-week HCN safety rules.
  9. Keep simple records â cost per bale, yield per hectare, and animal response drive your next season's crop choice.

Further Reading

  • FAO Grassland Index â species datasheets for tropical grasses and legumes
  • Feedipedia â open animal feed composition database (INRAE, CIRAD, AFZ, FAO)
  • ILRI Feed Assessment Tool (FEAST) â feed resource planning for African farms
  • KALRO (Kenya Agricultural & Livestock Research Organisation) â fodder agronomy and seed guidance
  • IITA â legume and cereal research for African farming systems

This Practical Reference is part of the RISE AFRICA Skills course Silage & Hay Making, Module: Selecting Fodder Crops for African Conditions. Always validate recommendations with your national extension service and local seed suppliers before large-scale planting.

quiz.q: Which grass is most drought-tolerant and suitable for dry areas with 400â800 mm rainfall?
quiz.explanation: Rhodes grass is known for its drought tolerance and ability to grow in dry areas with 400â800 mm annual rainfall.

quiz.q: What is the recommended cutting height for Napier grass for silage?
quiz.explanation: For silage, Napier grass is best cut at 1.5â2 m height for optimal yield and quality.

quiz.q: Which legume is best for hay in high-altitude areas with irrigation?
quiz.explanation: Lucerne (alfalfa) performs best in cooler, high-altitude areas with irrigation and well-drained soils.

quiz.q: What is the ideal moisture content for baling hay?
quiz.explanation: Hay should be baled at 15â18% moisture to prevent mould and spontaneous combustion.

quiz.q: Which crop is the best choice for silage in semi-arid areas with 400â800 mm rainfall?
quiz.explanation: Sorghum is more drought-tolerant than maize and yields well in semi-arid areas with 400â800 mm rainfall.

quiz.q: At what stage should maize be harvested for silage?
quiz.explanation: Maize for silage is harvested at dough stage when dry matter is 30â35% for best fermentation.

quiz.q: What is the main advantage of using groundnut haulms as fodder?
quiz.explanation: Groundnut haulms are high in protein (10â15%) and highly digestible, making them excellent fodder.

quiz.q: How can you improve the nutritive value of maize stover?
quiz.explanation: Treating maize stover with urea (4 kg urea in 100 L water per 100 kg stover) raises protein and digestibility.

quiz.q: Which of these is a drought-tolerant fodder crop for arid regions?
quiz.explanation: Pearl millet is the most drought-tolerant cereal, yielding well with only 300â500 mm rainfall.

quiz.q: What percentage of lablab should be mixed with maize for balanced silage?
quiz.explanation: A common mix is 70% maize and 30% lablab, which raises protein to 12â14%.

quiz.q: What is the ideal pH range for good silage?
quiz.explanation: Good silage has a pH of 3.8â4.5 due to lactic acid fermentation.

quiz.q: Which grass is shade-tolerant and can be intercropped with trees?
quiz.explanation: Guinea grass is shade-tolerant and can be grown under trees or in agroforestry systems.

quiz.q: What is the recommended spacing for planting Napier grass using stem cuttings?
quiz.explanation: Napier grass is planted at 50 cm x 100 cm spacing using 3-node stem cuttings.

quiz.q: Which legume is best for intercropping with maize for silage?
quiz.explanation: Lablab is an annual legume that can be intercropped with maize and ensiled together for balanced silage.

quiz.q: What is the main risk of feeding mouldy groundnut haulms?
quiz.explanation: Mouldy groundnut haulms can contain aflatoxins, which are toxic to livestock.

quiz.q: Which crop residue has the lowest protein content?
quiz.explanation: Rice straw is very low in protein (3â4%) and high in silica, making it less digestible.

quiz.q: What is the recommended urea treatment rate for 100 kg of maize stover?
options: A) 1 kg urea in 50 L water
B) 4 kg urea in 100 L water
C) 10 kg urea in 200 L water
D) 20 kg urea in 100 L water
quiz.explanation: Treat 100 kg stover with 4 kg urea dissolved in 100 L water to improve protein and digestibility.

quiz.q: Which fodder crop is 90% water and survives with 200 mm rainfall?
quiz.explanation: Spineless cactus is 90% water and highly drought-tolerant, surviving with only 200 mm rainfall.

quiz.q: What is the ideal dry matter content for silage?
quiz.explanation: Silage should be ensiled at 30â35% dry matter for optimal fermentation.

quiz.q: Which of these is a high-yielding perennial grass for silage?
quiz.explanation: Napier grass is a high-yielding perennial that can produce 20â40 tonnes dry matter per hectare per year.

quiz.q: What is the protein content of good lucerne hay?
quiz.explanation: Lucerne hay cut at 10% flowering has 16â20% protein.

quiz.q: Which crop is most commonly used for silage in Africa?
quiz.explanation: Maize is the most common silage crop in Africa due to its high energy and yield.

quiz.q: What is the recommended plant population for maize silage per hectare?
quiz.explanation: A good maize silage crop has about 53,000 plants per hectare (75 cm x 25 cm spacing).

quiz.q: Which legume is a trailing type suitable for mixing with grasses?
quiz.explanation: Desmodium is a trailing legume that works well in mixed pastures with grasses.

quiz.q: What is the main advantage of mixing crops for silage?
quiz.explanation: Mixing crops balances energy and protein, providing a more complete feed.

quiz.q: Which of these is a drought-tolerant legume for arid regions?
quiz.explanation: Lablab is drought-tolerant and can be grown in semi-arid areas with 600â1200 mm rainfall.

quiz.q: What is the recommended moisture content for chopping silage?
quiz.explanation: Silage should be chopped and ensiled at 30â35% dry matter (65â70% moisture).

quiz.q: Which crop residue is highest in protein?
quiz.explanation: Groundnut haulms contain 10â15% protein, higher than other common crop residues.

quiz.q: What is the purpose of adding molasses to silage?
quiz.explanation: Molasses provides sugars for lactic acid bacteria, improving fermentation.

quiz.q: Which fodder crop is best for very dry areas with less than 300 mm rainfall?
quiz.explanation: Cactus (Opuntia) is extremely drought-tolerant and can survive with 200 mm rainfall.
